newsitem.title: USA: Expert in Simpson trial suggests two-killer theory.
newsitem.headline: Expert in Simpson trial suggests two-killer theory.

text.p: An expert witness for the defence in the O.J. Simpson civil trial suggested on Monday that two attackers may have been responsible for the murders of the former football star's ex-wife and her friend.
Michael Baden, medical examiner for the New York State Police, also contradicted testimony by a plaintiffs' witness that cuts to Simpson's left hand were inflicted by the victims' fingernails.
And he told jurors that victim Ronald Goldman probably fought with his knife-wielding attacker for five to 10 minutes before succumbing to his fatal injuries.

Baden's testimony about the length of Goldman's death struggle dented the plaintiffs' theory that Simpson would have had time to kill Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman and still get back home in time to meet a limousine driver taking him to the airport.

The often graphic testimony about Goldman's final moments reduced his father, Fred, and sister, Kim, to tears as they sat in the front row of the courtroom. Simpson was acquitted in October 1995 of criminal charges in the June 12, 1994, murders. He is fighting a wrongful death lawsuit by the victims families, who seek monetary damages.

Baden said he reached the conclusion that more than one assailant was involved in the attack because "it would have been very difficult for a single perpetrator to control multiple victims in a public place."
"I can't understand how these two people were murdered and not yell out unless there were two people there," he said.

Baden also rejected a theory, advanced by Dr. Werner Spitz during the plaintiffs' case, that cuts found on Simpson's left hand in the days after the murders were inflicted by the fingernails of the victims as their killer held them from behind in a death grip.
Baden used photographs of the cuts in testifying that they were probably caused by "some sharp, irregular object" like broken glass.
That opinion supports Simpson's testimony that he broke a drinking glass in his Chicago hotel room after being informed by telephone of his ex-wife's death.
Baden told jurors Goldman was probably on his feet for five to 10 minutes after he was stabbed in the neck, as evidenced by a flow of blood running down his shirt and pants and into his shoe.

"Once this wound was inflicted in the neck ... Mr. Goldman was able to stand up and continue to struggle, perhaps for up to five minutes," he said. "It would take that much time for the oozing blood from the neck to reach the shoe Mr. Goldman was wearing."
He said the three other major injuries Goldman sustained produced little internal bleeding, evidence that his heart was faltering by the time they were inflicted.
Lawyers for the victims families asserted the murders happened about 10:35 to 10:40 p.m. Simpson was spotted in his driveway by the limousine driver, Alan Park, about 10:55 p.m.
On cross-examination Goldman family lawyer, Edward Medvene, attacked Baden's testimony that two killers were involved.
But the doctor, who will return to the witness stand Tuesday, refused to back away from the theory, saying: "I find it difficult to put it together with a single assailant."

Earlier in the day forensic expert Herb MacDonell testified blood could have been planted on Simpson's sock and that gloves similar to ones found at the murder scene and Simpson's estate did not shrink when soaked in blood.

In the dramatic high-point of the criminal trial, Simpson tried on the bloody gloves for the jury and held up his hands to show that they apparently did not fit. The prosecution contended the gloves belonged to Simpson and were worn by the killer. They had shrunk after being soaked in blood, the prosecutors argued.
